content.title: Establishing Clear and Logical Comparisons
content.overview: Logical comparisons ensure that a sentence clearly identifies which two items are being compared and that the qualities being compared are grammatically parallel and unambiguous.
learning_objectives: Identify the two primary items being compared in a sentence.
Recognize comparison markers such as 'than', 'as', and 'like'.
Apply parallel grammatical structure to multiple qualities within a comparison.
Eliminate ambiguity by ensuring modifiers and comparison markers clearly attach to the intended nouns.

sections.title: Identifying the Comparison Structure
sections.content: A logical comparison requires two distinct elements: the items being compared and a comparison marker. Common markers include 'than', 'as', and 'like'. To evaluate a sentence, first underline the two items. If the sentence lists multiple qualities (e.g., 'faster and more efficient'), both qualities must relate to the items in the same way. If the sentence structure makes it unclear which quality belongs to which item, the comparison is illogical or ambiguous.

sections.title: Maintaining Parallelism in Comparisons
sections.content: When comparing multiple attributes of an item to another, those attributes must use the same grammatical form. For example, if you use a comparative adjective like 'more accessible,' the subsequent quality should also be a comparative adjective like 'more innovative.' This consistency allows the comparison marker (like 'than') to apply to the entire group of qualities simultaneously.

sections.title: Resolving Ambiguity
sections.content: Ambiguity often occurs when a modifier or a second quality is placed too far from the noun it describes, or when the comparison marker is misplaced. To fix this, you may need to repeat a noun or rephrase the sentence so that the comparison marker clearly follows all listed qualities. A common ACT fix is to group all qualities together before the comparison marker: '[Item A] is [Quality 1] and [Quality 2] than [Item B].'

worked_examples.question:
Identify the error and choose the best revision: 'The new software is more user-friendly than the old version and its faster processing speed.'

A. NO CHANGE
B. more user-friendly and faster than the old version.
C. more user-friendly than the old version, with faster processing speed.
D. more user-friendly than the old version and its speed is faster.'
worked_examples.solution: 1. Identify items: 'new software' vs 'old version'. 2. Identify qualities: 'user-friendly' and 'processing speed'. 3. Check parallelism: 'more user-friendly' is a comparative adjective phrase, but 'its faster processing speed' is a noun phrase. They are not parallel. 4. Apply fix: Group the qualities. 'More user-friendly and faster' are both comparative adjectives. 5. Final check: 'The new software is more user-friendly and faster than the old version.' This clearly compares both traits to the old version. Choice B is correct.

common_mistakes: Comparing a quality to an item (e.g., 'The speed of the car is faster than the truck' instead of 'than the speed of the truck').
Mixing grammatical forms, such as pairing an adjective with a noun phrase in the same comparison.
Placing the comparison marker 'than' in the middle of a list of qualities, which can make the final quality seem like a separate, non-compared thought.
exam_tips: If a comparison sounds 'clunky' or 'off,' underline the two things being compared to see if they actually match.
Look for 'than'—if there are two adjectives before it, make sure they are both in the same form (e.g., both ending in -er or both preceded by 'more').
Watch out for 'than that of' or 'than those of' constructions; these are often used to ensure you are comparing a quality to a quality rather than a quality to an object.
content.recap: To establish a clear comparison, identify the two items and ensure all compared qualities use parallel grammatical forms. Place comparison markers so they apply to all intended qualities without creating ambiguity.

knowledge_claims.content: A logical comparison requires identifying two specific items and a comparison marker such as 'than', 'as', or 'like'.
Multiple qualities compared in a single sentence must use the same grammatical form, such as using two comparative adjectives.
To fix an ambiguous comparison, group all parallel qualities together before the comparison marker.
If a quality is placed after the comparison marker without being parallel, it may incorrectly appear as a separate detail rather than a compared trait.
It is an error to compare a specific attribute of one item (like 'height') directly to a whole different item (like 'a building') instead of that item's attribute.
A comparison is verified as logical if reading it aloud clearly links every listed quality to the correct target item relative to the second item.
Parallel form in comparisons means using consistent parts of speech, such as ensuring all compared traits are adjectives or all are noun phrases.
Repeating a noun or using a pronoun like 'that of' can resolve ambiguity when comparing specific traits of two different objects.
The trigger for checking comparison logic is seeing a sentence that compares two things while listing multiple qualities or items.
The comparison marker 'than' must reference a clear, singular target for the comparison to be valid.
When editing, underline the two items being compared to ensure the sentence structure supports a direct relationship between them.
A common trap is a choice that adds a quality as an extra detail (using 'with') instead of making it a parallel part of the comparison.

items.stem:
Practice form 1. Rina is editing a short report about a community garden.

Which comparison is logically complete?

options.A: The new sensor is more precise than the old design measures.
options.B: The precision of the new sensor is greater than the old sensor.
options.C: The new sensor is more precise than the old sensor.
options.D: The new sensor is more precise compared to measuring.

items.explanation: The correct choice directly applies the target skill: 建立清晰、合逻辑的比较结构.
